title: Command-line task manager
summary: A Python command-line tool to add, list, complete and search tasks, saved to a JSON file and covered by unit tests.
why: It proves you can take a small program from idea to a tested, documented tool that someone else can install and use. Reviewers see clean structure, file I/O, input validation and tests, which are the habits interns need from day one.
brief:
Build `tasks`, a command-line task manager in Python. Users run commands like `tasks add "Finish lab 3" --due 2026-10-20 --tag school`, `tasks list`, `tasks done 3` and `tasks search lab`. Tasks persist between runs in a JSON file in the user's home directory, or at a path set by an environment variable (which also makes testing easy).

Constraints: the app itself uses only the standard library (argparse, json, datetime, pathlib), with pytest for tests. Keep the core logic (a TaskStore class or a module of plain functions) separate from the command-line layer, so the logic can be tested without running the CLI. Handle bad input gracefully: an unknown task id, a malformed date, or a missing or corrupted data file should produce a clear message and a non-zero exit code, never a traceback.

Work in small commits with clear messages from the first day, and write the README as you go. This is the first project in the SWE track; the structure and testing habits you build here carry into every later project.

milestones.title: Core model and storage
tasks: Define a task (id, title, done, created, due, tags) as a dataclass
Write load and save functions for the JSON file, creating it if it is missing
Write add, list, complete and delete functions that work on the loaded tasks
milestones.doneWhen: From a Python shell you can add three tasks, save, restart the shell, load, and see the same three tasks.

milestones.title: Command-line interface
tasks: Use argparse subcommands: add, list, done, delete and search
Print a readable table for list, with overdue tasks marked
Exit with code 0 on success and 1 on user errors
milestones.doneWhen: Every subcommand works from the terminal, and `tasks --help` documents each one.

milestones.title: Tests
tasks: Write pytest tests for each core function using a temporary data file (the tmp_path fixture)
Test edge cases: empty list, unknown id, duplicate titles, bad dates and corrupted JSON
Add tests that call the CLI entry point with arguments and check the output and exit code
milestones.doneWhen: `pytest` passes with at least 20 tests that cover every subcommand and every error path.

milestones.title: Search, due dates and tags
tasks: Add case-insensitive search across titles and tags
Add --due with ISO dates and sort the list by due date
milestones.doneWhen: `tasks list --overdue` shows only past-due, incomplete tasks, verified by a test that fixes today's date to a known value.

milestones.title: Package and document
tasks: Add a pyproject.toml so `pip install .` creates a `tasks` command
Write a README with install steps, usage examples for every command and a short design section
Record a short terminal GIF or include sample output
milestones.doneWhen: A friend can clone the repository, follow the README and run `tasks add` in under five minutes.

stretch: Recurring tasks (daily or weekly) that regenerate when completed
A GitHub Actions workflow that runs the tests on every push
Store data in SQLite instead of JSON and write up the trade-offs
Write the data file safely: write to a temporary file, then rename it over the old one
rubric: A reviewer should see core logic separated from argument parsing, in modules with clear names
A reviewer should see `pytest` pass, with tests for normal use and for every error path
A reviewer should see bad input handled with a clear message and a non-zero exit code, never a traceback
A reviewer should see tasks survive a restart, saved in readable JSON
A reviewer should see a README that gets a new user from clone to first task in a few commands
A reviewer should see a history of small, descriptive commits rather than one large upload
showcase: README sections: one sentence on what it does, a terminal GIF or sample output, install, usage for each command, design notes (why JSON, how the code is split) and how to run the tests
Record a 20-second terminal GIF with a tool such as asciinema or vhs and put it near the top
Add a passing-tests badge once CI is set up
Pin it on GitHub while it is one of your best repositories; replace it as stronger projects arrive
resumeBullet: Built a Python command-line task manager with due dates, tags and search; wrote 30+ pytest tests covering every command and error path, and packaged it for pip install.
interviewTalkingPoints: Why you separated storage and logic from the CLI layer, and how that made testing easier
JSON file versus SQLite: what you chose and when you would switch
How you handled a corrupted or missing data file
How you tested date-dependent behavior such as overdue tasks (by passing in today's date)
